title: Fitting an oak window board to a masonry reveal
subtitle: Fix a solid hardwood window board (sill) to the internal face of a brick or block masonry window reveal
excerpt: How to fit a solid oak window board to a masonry window reveal. Covers measuring and cutting the board, fitting a timber packing frame, scribing the board to the plaster, securing with screws, and filling and oiling the finished board.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK joinery trade practice for hardwood window boards.

glossaryTerms.definition: The horizontal shelf fitted at the bottom of the internal window reveal, resting on the masonry sill and extending across the full reveal width with a slight overhang at the front. Also called a window sill or internal sill. In older properties window boards were typically 25 to 32 mm thick softwood painted white; oak is a premium replacement choice.

The process of transferring an irregular profile (an uneven plaster wall, a sloping floor) onto the timber that will butt against it, so the timber can be cut to fit exactly. A compass or profile gauge traces the irregularity; a saw or chisel removes the waste to the scribed line.

content.text: is fitted to the masonry sill inside the reveal with a slight projection beyond the reveal face. The rear edge butts against the window frame; the two side returns are
to the plaster on each jamb. Oak is harder to fit than softwood because it does not compress against irregularities.
Measure and cut the board to size

Measure the reveal width at the sill level. The board should fit between the two plaster reveals with the side returns cut to fit into the reveals and the front edge projecting 25 to 30 mm beyond the plaster face of the wall. Cut the board to the overall length (reveal width plus both side return depths) with the tenon saw. Mark and cut the side return shoulders with the tenon saw; use the chisel and mallet to pare the shoulder faces clean and square.

The masonry sill is rarely flat or level. Fix a packing frame of 25 x 50 mm softwood battens to the masonry to create a perfectly level surface for the board to rest on. Plug and screw the battens at 300 mm centres, using slate or hardboard packing pieces under the batten to level it precisely. Check the packing frame level across its length and width before fixing the board.
Scribe the board to the plaster

Place the board on the packing frame with the back edge hard against the window frame. Set a compass to the widest gap between the board side return and the plaster jamb. Run the compass along the plaster surface with the pencil marking a line on the board face that follows the contour of the plaster. Cut along the scribed line with a coping saw or tenon saw and pare to the line with the chisel. The scribed edge should now fit neatly against the plaster.

Fix the board from below through the packing frame with 50 mm Pozi screws. Counter-sink and counter-bore the screw holes and fill with matching oak pellets glued in flush. Sand the surface through 120 and 180 grit with the sanding block. Apply two coats of Danish oil or a hardwax oil (such as Osmo Polyx) to all faces of the board including the underside to reduce movement in service. Caulk any gap between the board rear edge and the window frame with a matching paintable caulk.

attrs.symptom: Board ends do not fit the reveals neatly despite scribing
attrs.cause: Reveals are not parallel, so each side needs individual scribing.
attrs.fix: Scribe each side separately, fitting one side first, then scribing the other to the fitted position.

attrs.symptom: Board lifts at the corners after a year or two
attrs.cause: The oak is moving in response to seasonal humidity changes and the fixings are not holding it flat.
attrs.fix: Slot the screw holes through the packing frame slightly to allow the board to move along its length. Do not use glue in addition to screws: glue restrains movement and causes splitting.
